title: Refuting “Reciting the Buddha with a Scattered Mind Still Ensures Rebirth”
author: Zhanran
excerpt: “The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind is scattered (scattered-mind recitation); cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.”

inline.s: “The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind is scattered
(scattered-mind recitation)
, cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.”

Question: Hongyuan Temple in Anhui published an essay by Master Zhisui titled “Reciting the Buddha with a Scattered Mind Still Ensures Rebirth,” excerpted from his Brief Commentary on the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra. Is this view correct?
Answer: The claim that “reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind still ensures rebirth” is gravely mistaken.
The condition for rebirth is:
ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at the moment of death.
(For details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
But scattered-mind recitation cannot accomplish this, and so it spoils the great matter of rebirth.
Hence Master Hanshan taught:
“The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind is scattered — cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.”
[Scattered-mind recitation] Reciting the Buddha while one’s thoughts wander.
[But scattered-mind recitation cannot accomplish it]
Scattered-mind recitation cannot attain ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at the moment of death.
Master Daochuo taught:
“The wise diligently gather the mind, and at death their thought does not scatter; those who have not trained the mind to be single-pointed
(scattered-mind recitation is precisely “not training the mind to be single-pointed”)
at death will surely be scattered
(For details, see
Master Daochuo’s Pure Practice Teachings
[The mouth recites Amitabha, the mind is scattered — cry your throat raw and it is all in vain] The full verse reads:

“Reciting the Buddha is easy, a faithful mind is hard; when mouth and mind are not one, it is all in vain. The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind is scattered — cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.”
Translation:

Reciting the Buddha is easy but a truthful, faithful mind is hard. When mouth and mind are not one (the mind is not faithful: the mouth recites the Buddha while the mind thinks of other things), it is all idle (all effort is wasted). The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind thinks of other things — cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.
(For details, see
Commentary on the Song of Wasted Idleness

[Faithful/truthful] Means honest, without deceit. “Faithful mind” means a truthful, faithful mind; when mouth and mind are not one, it is false. Hence the next line reads, “when mouth and mind are not one, it is all in vain.”

The Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra is Master Ouyi’s commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra. In the Amitabha Sūtra, Śākyamuni Buddha taught the Dharma-gate of liberation within this very life, by which one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss —
faith and vows, and the upholding of the Name with single-minded, undistracted concentration

. Moreover, this Dharma-gate is praised in unison by all the Buddhas of the various directions (including, of course, Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss). Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are certain to be remembered and protected by all the Buddhas of the various directions (including, of course, Amitabha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss); and those who practice as taught are certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (For details, see
Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra as Spoken by the Buddha
and
Commentary on the Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Reception

) In the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra, Master Ouyi likewise teaches that reciting the Buddha with single-minded, undistracted concentration is certain to bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (For details, see
Commentary on the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra
) Moreover, regarding scattered-mind recitation, Master Ouyi further taught clearly:
although scattered-mind recitation can remove offenses,
it does not ensure rebirth
, and he pointed out that only by reciting to the point of single-minded, undistracted concentration can one be assured of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
(Original text:
“Question: Does reciting the name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? Answer: The merit of the name is inconceivable — how could it not remove offenses?
But it does not ensure rebirth
Only when one recites to the point of single-minded, undistracted concentration
is it like a strong man breaking out through an encirclement, whom no three armies can restrain.”
) When explaining faith, vows, and practice, Master Ouyi also pointed out clearly:
“Without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, one cannot fulfill one’s vows or realize what one believes.
Practice means upholding the Name with single-minded, undistracted concentration
Thus, the Amitabha Sūtra says
reciting the Buddha with single-minded, undistracted concentration is certain to bring rebirth
, and the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra, which comments on the Amitabha Sūtra, likewise says
reciting the Buddha with single-minded, undistracted concentration is certain to bring rebirth
, and further says
scattered-mind recitation does not ensure rebirth
Yet the Brief Commentary on the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra, which comments on the Essential Explanation, openly declares:
one need not
attain single-minded, undistracted concentration; “
reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind still ensures rebirth

.” How can this be called a commentary on the sūtras and treatises? It is outright slander of the sūtras and treatises, a brazen negation of the Amitabha Sūtra and the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra. Have they never considered
how grave are the consequences of slandering the Buddha and the Dharma!
The core question of Pure Land practice is:
the principle of rebirth
— how can one be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
So what is the principle of rebirth? The principle of rebirth is:
right mindfulness at the moment of death, evoking the Buddha’s coming to welcome one.
(For details, see
The Principle of Rebirth
essay
.) Thus both Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo taught:
ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at the moment of death bring rebirth.
(For details, see
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings
Master Daochuo’s Pure Practice Teachings
) Moreover, in his Collection on the Land of Peace and Bliss, Master Daochuo explained clearly the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow (Amitabha’s Fundamental Vow):
“If there are sentient beings who, even if they have committed evil all their lives,
at the moment of death, with ten recitations in uninterrupted succession, call my name
, and if they should fail to be reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
Here Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of “even ten recitations” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the moment of death, with ten recitations in uninterrupted succession, calling my name.

Therefore, in daily practice one must earnestly achieve ten recitations in uninterrupted succession until it becomes second nature, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Hence Master Shandao, a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, taught:
“Precisely because name-recitation is easy
(precisely because reciting the name is easier than contemplating the Buddha)
, an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life
(one who practices thus for life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
(For details, see
The Eighteenth Vow
Ten Recitations at Death: Uninterrupted Succession Brings Rebirth
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
[Right mindfulness at death, evoking the Buddha’s coming to welcome one] At the moment of death, maintaining
the right mindfulness of reciting the Buddha,
one responds in mutual resonance with the Buddha, and the Buddha comes to lead one forth. Hence Master Shandao, a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, taught:
“An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Both Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo taught:
ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at the moment of death bring rebirth.
(For details, see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings
Master Daochuo’s Pure Practice Teachings
) [Mutual resonance] The response of sentient beings and the answering of Amitabha Buddha intermingle and connect.
[Become second nature through repeated practice] Through continuous, repeated practice, ten recitations in uninterrupted succession become instinctive.

The crux of scattered-mind recitation is this: can scattered-mind recitation, which runs counter to the Buddha’s teaching and the patriarchs’ instructions, achieve ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at the moment of death? And ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at death is the condition for rebirth
(for details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth
On this point,
Master Daochuo long ago gave clear instruction:
“The wise diligently gather the mind
(reciting the Buddha single-mindedly in daily life)
, and at death their thought does not scatter;
those who have not trained the mind to be single-pointed
(reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind in daily life)
, at death will surely be scattered
(For details, see
Master Daochuo’s Pure Practice Teachings
Master Yongming, a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, taught:
The present is the cause, the moment of death is the result; the cause must be true, so that the result will not be vain.
If you wish
ten recitations to be accomplished at the moment of death,
then prepare the bridge and ford in advance
(make thorough preparation beforehand)
, gather and accumulate merit, and dedicate it to that moment
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
; if not one recitation is lacking, then you need have no worry.”

(Collected Writings on the Ten Thousand Good Deeds Returning to One) Therefore, the possibility of rebirth for one who recites with a scattered mind is negligible, not “surely reborn”; those who recite the Buddha must be on their guard
Master Hanshan said:
“The mouth recites Amitabha while the mind is scattered — cry your throat raw, and it is all in vain.”
This is a lesson of blood and tears about scattered-mind recitation, proven by practice over a thousand years
. Hence Master Hanshan, accomplished in both Chan and Pure Land, earnestly admonished those who recite the Buddha in his Song of Wasted Idleness (
see
Master Hanshan: The Song of Wasted Idleness (with Commentary)

). For example, the essay Getting Clear About the Conditions for Rebirth records: “Recently someone told me, with great anxiety and heaviness, that the head of a certain large assisted-recitation group in Taiwan was in a very poor state at the moment of death and did not attain rebirth in the West. And someone else said dejectedly that a certain master had bowed to the Buddha two and a half million times, yet at death was still not well, and likely did not attain rebirth in the West either.” Are such lessons not painful enough? As for why scattered-mind recitation does not ensure rebirth, for its reasoning and basis see
Does Scattered-Mind Recitation Also Ensure Rebirth?

[Master Hanshan, accomplished in both Chan and Pure Land] To help Buddhist practitioners end birth and death in this very life, Master Hanshan everywhere pointed to the Pure Land, and all his life advocated and promoted the Pure Land Dharma-gate with perfect clarity of principle and practice. Moreover, he set an example himself, seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and attaining splendid accomplishment (see the Records of Pure Land Sages). And because his past vows were not yet fulfilled, he was reborn again as the tenth Pure Land patriarch, Master Xingce. Master Yinguang praised him, saying:
“Hanshan’s past vows were not yet repaid, so he appeared again as Jieliu
(Master Xingce)
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
The Tenth Pure Land Patriarch of the Qing, Master Xingce of Puren Temple on Mount Yu) (For details, see
Master Hanshan: A Patriarch of Both Chan and Pure Land
Since Master Huijing,

Master Jingzong, Master Zhisui, and their like constantly profess to revere Masters Tanluan, Daochuo, and Shandao as their patriarchs, why have they never taught the faithful these patriarchs’ supremely important instructions on how to attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss:

“Ten recitations at death: an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth.” “Ten recitations in uninterrupted succession, practiced until second nature.” “If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”

Instead, they stand in direct opposition to the patriarchs and vigorously propagate the false doctrines that “name-recitation ensures rebirth,” “reciting with a scattered mind still ensures rebirth,” and “faith and vows alone ensure rebirth”
In doing so, you not only harm the faithful but also harm yourselves.
Rebirth is a matter of great consequence
and I truly hope that you,
with the
utterly sincere mind
of a disciple of the Buddha,
will faithfully
study the treatises and instructions of Masters Tanluan, Daochuo, and Shandao, rather than cherry-picking passages for some private purpose.
Driven by faith and vows, you should teach the faithful with the true Dharma of Masters Tanluan, Daochuo, and Shandao
(how supremely excellent that would be!)
; rather than, under the sway of karmic force, deluding the faithful with the false Dharma of the Primal Vow school.
For a Buddhist practitioner,
the utterly sincere mind
is of the utmost importance; the karma of body, speech, and mind, and the practice and understanding one cultivates,
must all be done with a true and real mind
. Master Shandao taught:

“The sūtra says: ‘First, the utterly sincere mind.’ ‘Utterly’ means true; ‘sincere’ means real. This is to make clear that the karma of body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings, and the practice and understanding they cultivate,
must all be done with a true and real mind

. One must not outwardly display an appearance of virtue, goodness, and diligence while inwardly harboring falsity — greed, anger, deviousness, and deceit in a hundred forms. Such evil nature, hard to assail, is like snakes and scorpions. Although the three kinds of karma arise, they are called good deeds mixed with poison, also called false practice, and cannot be called true karma. If one settles the mind and undertakes practice in this way, even if one painfully disciplines body and mind, hastening and toiling through the twelve periods of day and night as though one’s head were on fire, all of it is called good deeds mixed with poison.
To wish to dedicate such poison-mixed practice toward rebirth in that Buddha’s pure land is absolutely impossible.

Why? Precisely because when Amitabha Buddha practiced the bodhisattva path in his causal stage, even in a single thought or a single instant, the three kinds of karma he cultivated were all done with a true and real mind; everything he did and sought was likewise true.”
(Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles)
As to how one can attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, Master Shandao explained it with perfect clarity:
“Precisely because name-recitation is easy,
an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth

. If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. ...... May all people reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must rouse your mind and restrain yourself, never ceasing by day or night. When the preceding thought comes to an end, the following thought is reborn. Forever receiving the Dharma-joy of the unconditioned, until one attains Buddhahood — is this not delightful!”
(For details, see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

[Precisely because name-recitation is easy] Precisely because upholding the Name in recitation is easier to accomplish than contemplating the Buddha. [An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth] At the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Those who practice until the end of life] Those who practice thus all their lives.

[Rouse your mind and restrain yourself] To rouse the mind is to spur it to do what ought to be done; to restrain oneself is to keep oneself from doing what ought not to be done. These four words, “rouse the mind and restrain yourself,” are a mighty weapon for overcoming hardship and sweeping away obstacles.
[Never cease by day or night] By day or night, never let the continuation of recitation thought after thought come to a stop.
Master Shandao is a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, and his instructions we must reverently practice. If one willfully distorts them or sings a contrary tune, the consequence is this:
not only will one fail to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but one will end up slandering the Buddha and the Dharma.

[Singing a contrary tune] Master Shandao, a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, taught: “An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth.” Yet the Primal Vow school vigorously propagates: “Name-recitation ensures rebirth,” “reciting with a scattered mind still ensures rebirth.”

The immense harm of propagating “name-recitation ensures rebirth,” “reciting with a scattered mind still ensures rebirth,” and “faith and vows alone ensure rebirth” lies in this: it misleads practitioners onto a wrong path, causing them not only to waste this life but also to implant wrong views in the ālaya consciousness, so that in life after life they remain subject to its latent influence:
“Delighting in inferior dharmas, they conceive wrong views within right views, and conceive right views within wrong views.”
(Buddha Treasury Sūtra)

Observe closely those people who find the true Dharma and right views grating to the ear, yet fervently embrace false dharmas and wrong views, and you will see how terrifying this latent influence — karmic force — truly is: from the false they enter deeper into the false, and set out on a road of no return! Hence the ancients said:
“Better a thousand years without awakening than a single day on the wrong path.”
Conversely, if we teach students with the true Dharma of
“right mindfulness at death, evoking the Buddha’s coming to welcome one,”
“ten recitations at death: an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth,”
“ten recitations in uninterrupted succession, practiced until second nature,”
and
“if one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn,”

then they can end birth and death in this very life. Even if in this life they do not achieve ten recitations in uninterrupted succession at death, the right view implanted in the ālaya consciousness will blossom and bear fruit in lives to come.

Question: Why did Chan Master Sixin say, “Amitabha is very easy to recite, and the Pure Land very easy to reach. If you recite the Buddha and are not reborn in the Pure Land, may this old monk fall into the hell of tongues being pulled out”?

Answer: For the Chan school, it is indeed true that “Amitabha is very easy to recite, and the Pure Land very easy to reach.” Hence the Essential Rules of the Monastery, first instituted by Master Baizhang, opens with the words:
“A monastery flourishes through having no affairs; practice is most secure through reciting the Buddha.”

For to end birth and death and escape saṃsāra through Chan investigation, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing, and the seeing of one’s true nature, and then undertake the work of nurturing and sustaining it, until the afflictions of views and of thought are entirely severed — only then can one end birth and death and escape saṃsāra. A Chan practitioner who has reached “the ten thousand thoughts returning to one” is still only at the initial stage of Chan investigation, still a long way from fully severing the afflictions of views and of thought; to end birth and death through Chan practice alone is extremely difficult and by no means assured. But if such practitioners turn to reciting the Buddha, they can attain single-minded, undistracted recitation within a day, or within seven days at most, and thereby ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — and thus end birth and death and escape saṃsāra. Therefore Chan Master Sixin urged them to turn to Pure Land practice, saying:

“Amitabha is very easy to recite, and the Pure Land very easy to reach. If you recite the Buddha and are not reborn in the Pure Land, may this old monk fall into the hell of tongues being pulled out.”

[Monastery] A Chan Buddhist monastery, as in the saying “Mazu established the monasteries, Baizhang established the regulations.” Later it came to refer broadly to large temples. [Mazu established the monasteries] In the first hundred or so years after the founding of Chan, Chan monks merely transmitted the Dharma to one another, mostly dwelling beneath rocky caves or lodging in Vinaya-school monasteries, where constant friction with the old rules prevented them from settling down to practice the Way. So Mazu (Chan Master Daoyi) resolved to found monastery grounds, establishing a separate Chan residence so that the monks of the Chan school could gather and live together in practice. [Baizhang established the regulations] Chan Master Baizhang drew up the Essential Rules of the Monastery, thereby creating the regulations of the Chan school.
Question: Nowadays some groups and websites use the name “Pure Land school,”
such as Pure Land school Hongyuan Temple, Pure Land school
Pure Land school gateway
China Pure Land school
Global Pure Land school gateway website, the Chinese Pure Land school Association, and the like
. What is going on here?
Answer: This is all the doing of Master Huijing of the Primal Vow school
(for this man’s background, see
What Is the Primal Vow School?
— his trickery.

The term “Pure Land school” originally referred to the school among the ten schools of Buddhism that specializes in reciting the Buddha and seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, tracing its founding patriarch to Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty;
it is a great school that has stood alongside the Chan school for a thousand years.

Their so-called Primal Vow school, however, is nothing more than a tiny sect, yet Master Huijing has had the audacity to name it “Pure Land school,” as though they were the entire Pure Land school! This is a deliberate creation of confusion — passing off fish eyes for pearls, the false for the true — to deceive people who do not know the truth, especially beginners, so that they mistake this sect for the Pure Land school and climb aboard a pirate ship. — This is the very means by which the Primal Vow school makes its living:
deception!
Disciples of the Buddha must keep their eyes open:
whenever they encounter groups and websites named after the “Pure Land school,” they must carefully discern whether it is the Primal Vow school, lest they be taken in and deceived.

The method of discernment is also simple: if the group is led by Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and their like, and promotes the views and theories of the Primal Vow school — such as the Pure Land school Hongyuan Temple, Pure Land school
Pure Land school gateway
China Pure Land school

Global Pure Land school gateway website, the Chinese Pure Land school Association, and so on — then it is the Primal Vow school, a heretical path cloaked in Buddhism, and not the true Pure Land school.
Their true names should be: Primal Vow school Hongyuan Temple, China Primal Vow school
Global gateway website, the Chinese Primal Vow school Association, and so on — only then do the name and the reality match.

[The ten schools] The Abhidharmakośa school, the Satyasiddhi school, the Chan school, the Tiantai school, the Huayan school, the Mantra school, the Dharma-Characteristics school, the Pure Land school, the Vinaya school, and the Three Treatises school. [The views and theories of the Primal Vow school] For details, see
The Primal Vow School Is a Heretical Path Cloaked in Buddhism
